Direct answer

Volume × density = grams

Weight = material volume × density. A solid 10cm³ print in PLA at 1.24g/cm³ weighs 12.4g. The same volume in ABS at 1.04g/cm³ weighs 10.4g — about 16% lighter for the same shape. For a hollow FDM part, subtract the cavity behind the wall and count only the infill percentage of what is left. The calculator does each step live.

Once you have grams, the filament cost calculator turns that into money, including optional electricity.

The math

125.0 cm³ outer · 33.3 cm³ material (1.2mm wall · 15% infill) × 1.24 g/cm³ = 41.3 g

This is an estimate

Densities are typical published values — brand-to-brand variation is about ±2%, and colour dyes make no practical difference. Hollow math assumes a uniform wall and even infill, so it will not match a print with heavy supports, a purge tower or a brim. The print-time baseline is a planning figure, not a slicer estimate.

Material density reference

MaterialDensityTypical use
PLA1.24 g/cm³The default for miniatures — cheap, stiff, crisp detail
PETG1.27 g/cm³Tough and slightly heavier than PLA — terrain and functional parts
ABS1.04 g/cm³Lightest common filament — needs an enclosure
ASA1.07 g/cm³UV-stable ABS alternative for outdoor prints
TPU1.21 g/cm³Flexible rubber-like material — banners, tracks, tires
Nylon (PA12)1.14 g/cm³Strong and slightly hygroscopic — engineering parts
Polycarbonate (PC)1.2 g/cm³High-heat engineering filament
PLA-CF1.27 g/cm³Carbon-fibre filled PLA — fillers push the density up
Resin — Standard1.1 g/cm³General purpose photopolymer — usually printed solid
Resin — Tough1.12 g/cm³Higher impact resistance for functional resin parts
Resin — ABS-Like1.15 g/cm³The most common upgrade resin for miniatures
Resin — Flexible1.1 g/cm³Rubber-like photopolymer for tires and gaskets

How I use this before slicing

  1. 1

    Enter dimensions or paste a volume

    Measure the bounding box, pick box, cylinder, sphere or tube, and type the numbers. If your slicer already reports volume in cm³, switch to Direct volume.

  2. 2

    Match the material and shell

    Pick your filament so the density is right, then choose Solid for a solid part or Hollow with the wall and infill your profile actually uses.

  3. 3

    Check the grams against your roll

    The tool reports prints per spool and the filament cost of this one. If the number is close to what is left on your roll, drop the infill or open the full cost calculator.

Filament density FAQ

How do you calculate filament weight from volume?

Weight = volume × density. A 10cm³ solid model in PLA at 1.24g/cm³ weighs 12.4g. For a hollow FDM print, subtract the interior behind the wall thickness, then add only the chosen infill percentage of what remains.

What is the density of PLA, PETG, ABS and resin?

PLA is 1.24g/cm³, PETG 1.27, ABS 1.04, ASA 1.07, TPU 1.21 and nylon about 1.14. Standard resin sits near 1.10 and ABS-like resin around 1.15. Denser material means a heavier print at the same volume.

Why does hollow + infill cut the weight so much?

Most FDM prints are shells, not solids. The calculator takes the outer volume, subtracts the cavity behind your wall thickness, and fills only a fraction of that cavity. A 50mm cube with a 1.2mm wall at 15% infill uses a small fraction of the filament a solid cube would need.

Does colour or additives change density?

Colour pigment makes no practical difference. Fillers do: carbon-fibre blends such as PLA-CF are slightly denser than base PLA, which is why they have their own preset in the table below.

How accurate is the print time estimate?

It is a planning baseline, not a slicer replacement. Time is material volume multiplied by a minutes-per-cm³ constant for the chosen quality preset. Supports, wall count, infill pattern and speed profiles all move the real number, so take the slicer estimate as final.
